key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn to trigger tools from superficial cues instead of true task need, but a tool-necessity reward can reduce this shortcut behavior.
engineering_relevance: For reliable agentic systems, tool-routing policies should be evaluated and rewarded at the decision level to prevent brittle cue-driven actions.
method: Built controlled synthetic QA and math environments with cue–tool correlations during training.
Tested counterfactual cases where cues appeared but the associated tool was unnecessary.
Added dense LLM-judge reward for each tool call to score tool necessity.
evidence_signal: Across counterfactual evaluations, spurious tool invocation rose by up to 39% under shortcut learning, and the failure appeared mainly after the agent had already learned the target tool well.
watch_item: An LLM-based necessity judge may itself introduce cost, latency, or bias, so its reliability must be validated carefully in deployment.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
